conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in because you’ve been feeling weak, nauseous, and itchy. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been a rough week. I’ve had this whole-body pain, and the itching is driving me crazy. I’ve also been dizzy and nauseous. My energy is just gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned your kidney doctor told you it was time to start dialysis, but it hadn’t started yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I was supposed to start last month, but my nephrologist said to wait. Now I feel worse than ever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function has declined—your creatinine is 3.8 and BUN is 137. That explains the nausea, itching, and fatigue. These are signs of uremia, which means toxins are building up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I really need dialysis now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your transplanted kidney isn’t working anymore, and your body can’t clear waste on its own. We’ll start dialysis during this admission to help you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about it. Is it painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not painful. First, we’ll place a temporary dialysis catheter in your neck. That’s done by a specialist tomorrow morning. You’ll get some sedation so you’ll be comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… and then what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the catheter is in, we’ll start dialysis. It takes a few hours and you can rest or watch TV. Most people start feeling better after the first session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been making urine though. Does that mean my kidneys still work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still making urine, which is good, but it’s not enough to clear the toxins. Your labs show your kidneys aren’t filtering properly, even if they’re still producing some urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my potassium? I remember that can be dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your potassium was low at 3.1 when you came in, not high. We’ll monitor it closely. Dialysis can affect potassium, so we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I have heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart, but no fluid in the lungs. That’s good. We’ll keep monitoring your blood pressure and volume status, especially with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today we’re going to place the dialysis catheter in your neck. The radiology team will do it with ultrasound and X-ray guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be given medication to help you relax and feel comfortable. You’ll be awake but drowsy. The team will numb the area, so you shouldn’t feel pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. The catheter is in place in your left internal jugular vein, and it’s ready to use. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt some pressure, but no pain. I’m glad it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll start your first dialysis session this afternoon. It’ll take about three hours. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit tired, but the itching is already less. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Dialysis is helping clear the toxins. We’ll do it again tomorrow and the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show improvement. Your creatinine dropped to 3.0 and BUN to 58. Your acid levels are also correcting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means dialysis is working. We also checked your hepatitis and TB tests—they’re negative, so you’re cleared for outpatient dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain? My back and leg still hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your oxycodone for breakthrough pain. We’ve also increased your gabapentin to 300 mg at night to help with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the itching? It’s better, but still there sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added hydroxyzine, an antihistamine you can take every six hours as needed. It should help more now that dialysis is removing the irritants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two dialysis sessions and are doing well. Your creatinine is now 2.7 and BUN 40. Your potassium is stable at 3.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Less nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll do one more session tomorrow, then plan for discharge. You’ll continue dialysis as an outpatient three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to the dialysis center at Mercy General. Your first appointment is this Friday at 6 PM. We’ve set everything up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last dialysis session went smoothly. Labs this morning show your creatinine is 2.6 and bicarbonate is normal at 28. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stop sodium bicarbonate—it’s no longer needed with dialysis. You’re now on Nephrocaps, a vitamin made for dialysis patients. Take it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizure medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue levetiracetam twice daily. Plus, you’ll take an extra 250 mg dose after each dialysis session to maintain the level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my fistula? My right arm one isn’t working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled you with vascular surgery. They’ll evaluate your right arm veins. The basilic vein looks usable, so they may create a new fistula there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health meds? I’ve been anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on paroxetine and quetiapine. Keep taking them. We’ve also kept your pain agreement with Dr. Evans—oxycodone is still PRN for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’ll have home health support for a few days to check your catheter site and help with transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really scared at first, but I feel so much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember to weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds. Keep all your follow-up appointments—with nephrology, vascular surgery, and pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need anything.
